The temple fair came to the village every Kartik, and this year Manoj's friends were going on their own. Manoj, fifteen, had lived with a heart condition since he was small.
"He'll stay home," said his elder brother Jeevan, before Manoj could open his mouth. "Too much crowd."
Manoj stared at the floor. Jeevan carried his school bag, answered the doctor's questions for him, even chose his sweets. Manoj knew it was love. It still felt like a rope around his chest.
That night he found Jeevan by the cowshed. "Bhaiya, ask me first. I know my body. I'll go with Sunil and Hari, take your phone, sit down if I get tired, and be back before the fireworks."
Jeevan was quiet for a long time. "And you'll call me if anything feels wrong?"
"Promise."
"Then go."

qa.q: Where did Manoj find Jeevan that night?
qa.a: He found Jeevan by the cowshed.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel when Jeevan decided for him?
qa.a: He felt smothered and small, like a rope around his chest, even though he knew it was love.

qa.q: What turned the situation around?
qa.a: Manoj asked to be consulted and offered a safe plan, and Jeevan let him take that reasonable risk.

qa.q: Why might Jeevan be so protective of his younger brother?
qa.a: He loves Manoj and is afraid something will happen in a crowd, so he tries to control every choice.

grounding: It shows a teenager with a long-term condition feeling smothered by a loving, fearful brother, and being trusted with a safe plan once he is included.

Abebe wheeled into the kitchen of their flat in Addis Ababa and waited until his mother, Hana, finished stirring the stew.
"Emaye, the coding club meets across town on Saturdays. I want to go by minibus."
Hana's spoon stopped. "Alone? No. I'll drive you."
"You drive me everywhere. You talk to my teachers for me. I'm sixteen."
"Because I worry about you. The ramps, the crowds..."
"I know. But when you decide everything, I feel like a little boy."
Hana sat down. Her eyes were wet. "Then tell me your plan."
He had one: which minibus had the ramp, where to wait, a message when he arrived. "First Saturday, cousin Dawit comes along. After that, just me."
She breathed out slowly. "Message me every time."
"Every time."

qa.a: He wants to go to the coding club across town on Saturdays.

qa.q: How does Abebe feel when his mother decides everything?
qa.a: He feels frustrated and treated like a little boy, even though he knows she worries.

qa.q: Which choice helped Hana and Abebe move forward?
qa.a: Asking him for his plan and agreeing on a gradual first trip with his cousin respected his growing independence while keeping it safe.

qa.q: What is this conversation like for Hana?
qa.a: It is hard and emotional for her, as her eyes are wet, because her fear pulls against wanting him to grow up.

grounding: It shows a disabled teenager who feels smothered by a loving, fearful mother, and how involving him in the plan allows a safe risk.

The bank in the small town of Sironj had six steep steps and no ramp. Gopika, twenty, stopped her wheelchair at the bottom and looked up.
"Rules, madam," said the guard. "Staff cannot bring forms down."
Her friend Parveen went in and asked the manager to come out. He came, but he spoke only to Parveen. "What does she need?"
Gopika felt the old heat in her cheeks. Then she said, clearly, "Please speak to me. It's my account."
The manager blinked and turned. They finished the form on the bench outside.
At home Gopika wrote a letter to the bank asking for a ramp. "It's not me who's the problem," she told Parveen. "It's the steps."
Parveen nodded. "Next time I'll stand back and let you talk."

qa.q: How many steps did the bank have?
qa.a: The bank had six steep steps and no ramp.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel when the manager spoke only to Parveen?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and angry, with heat in her cheeks, but she was also determined to be spoken to directly.

qa.q: What wise step did Gopika take after the visit?
qa.a: She wrote a letter asking for a ramp, treating the steps as the bank's barrier, not her failing.

qa.q: How might Parveen see Parveen's own part in the visit?
qa.a: Parveen realises that stepping in to speak made the manager ignore Gopika, so next time Parveen will stand back.

The waiter in the Lisbon café smiled at Beatriz and asked, "And what would she like?"
Vera, folding her white cane, answered before Beatriz could. "She would like a coffee with milk and an almond tart, thanks."
The waiter mumbled sorry and hurried off. Beatriz winced. "I'm sorry. I should have said something."
"You can just look at the menu. I'll handle my own order," Vera said, half laughing, half tired.
The bigger problem was waiting at the university. That morning the exam office had told Vera that application forms had to be handwritten, no exceptions. She had spent the bus ride feeling stupid.
Now, stirring her coffee, she said, "It's not me. It's their form." She emailed the disability office asking for a digital copy. By evening, they had sent one.

Last Tuesday, I found my old dance photos while cleaning the cupboard. I sat on the floor and cried. Before my illness, I'd planned to open a studio. Now I walk with a stick on bad days.
By noon I was furious. The bus driver pulled away before I'd got both feet on the step, and I stood on the road shaking.

I called Pradeep and said, "Is it mad to feel all of that in one day?"

At the community centre in Mysuru, Irfan had volunteered for six months before his hearing got worse. Harsha, the coordinator, called him into the office.
"I've noticed the Monday meetings are harder for you now," Harsha said, facing him and speaking clearly. "What would help? You tell me."
Irfan thought. "Sit me where I can see faces. And switch on captions for the video calls."
"Done. Anything else?"
"Don't make an announcement."
"I wasn't planning to."
The next Monday, the chairs were in a circle and captions were on. When a new volunteer said, "Irfan, you're so brave to keep coming," Harsha simply moved to the agenda.
Weeks later, captions were still on every call. Irfan noticed that most. Harsha had never once forgotten.

Vandana

Joseph's broken leg was in its fifth week, the hostel lift had been broken for three days, and his roommate Jatin was away for exams. Joseph lived on the third floor.

"I'm useless. I can't even get down for food."
"You're not useless. You're healing. What did the physio say?"
"Small exercises every day. Crutches on stairs."
"Then do that. I'll ask the mess to send dinner up till I'm back."
